text.p: Following are some of the leading stories in the Swedish papers this morning. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.

- Sweden's minority government and its informal cooperation partner the Centre Party promise large tax cuts and benefit increases in the years after the 1998 general election, according to the government's spring budget proposal.
- Investor, the key holding company in the Wallenberg family's financial empire, will focus more on the profitability of companies it holds stakes in, chief executive Claes Dahlback said.
- The shoe business is back on its feet with figures showing Swedes spending between 9.5 percent and 11.5 percent more on shoes in recent months than in the corresponding period last year.
- With a 16.3 billion crown five-point spending programme and talk about a stronger economy, the Swedish government wants to combat unemployment, according to its spring budget proposal.
- It remains unclear who, on Monday, sold most of the 30 million share stake in Swedish power company Sydkraft to German electricity group Hamburgische Electricitaets-Werke (HEW).

Swedish pension company SPP announced it had sold 2.8 million shares and insurer Skandia said it had sold around 90 percent of its 5.1 million C shares in Sydkraft. Insurance company Trygg-Hansa confirmed it sold some of its seven million Sydkraft shares.

- As a large owner of banking group S-E-Banken, investment company Investor wants to contribute to sensible structural changes, its chief executive Claes Dahlback said, forecasting a halving of the number of large Swedish banks in the future.
- Entrepreneurs critisised the Swedish government's spring budget proposal, saying changes for small companies were not sufficient.

- Investor, the key investment company in the Wallenberg family's financial empire, wants to split up operations in banking group S-E-Banken and see through two mergers, analysts said. This would explain why Investor has doubled its stake in the bank to 9.2 percent of capital, they said.

- Swedish rolling bearing maker SKF reported a profit after financial items of 501 million crowns for the first quarter of 1997, almost 22 percent lower than market expectations of 639 million crowns.
